page: Vultr voc-c-16c-32gb-300s-amd is an instance in the Optimized Cloud Compute family, configured with a compute-leaning resource ratio. The server features 16 dedicated virtual CPUs (8 physical cores with 2 threads per core) powered by an AMD EPYC processor running at a base clock speed of 2.0 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. Cache provisions include 32 KB L1d, 0.5 MB L2, and 16 MB L3 cache. Memory capacity is set at 32.0 GB RAM, delivering a 1:2 ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU. Local storage is bundled as a 300 GB NVMe SSD, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address without integrated GPU acceleration.

Benchmark profiles show strong single-threaded throughput, with a Geekbench single-core score of 2,168.0 and a stress-ng single-core score of 2,935.67, both placing in the top 25 percent. Highly parallel tasks yield steady mid-tier results, including a Geekbench multi-core rating of 15,777.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 33,071.36. Memory bandwidth reaches 149.65 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads and 71.14 GB/sec for writes. The platform also demonstrates efficient text-focused processing, achieving 347.96 tokens per second in small model LLM text generation (top 10 percent) and strong performance in Geekbench image and text processing tests.

With its 1:2 RAM-to-CPU distribution, voc-c-16c-32gb-300s-amd favors compute density over large in-memory capacities. This configuration presents a cost-efficient profile for CPU-bound tasks that do not demand extensive RAM footprint or dedicated accelerators. Ideal workloads include continuous integration pipelines, software compilation suites, mid-sized relational database engines, static web serving clusters, and CPU-based lightweight model inference.

It includes 32.0 GB of system memory, yielding a 1:2 allocation of 2.0 GB per vCPU, paired with a bundled 300 GB NVMe SSD and one public IPv4 address, but lacks a dedicated GPU. Performance tests show strong single-core results, registering 2,168.0 in Geekbench single-core and top-tier token generation on lightweight language models, while multi-core compute and memory metrics register mid-tier consistency across synthetic benchmarks. The instance provides a cost-efficient architecture for CPU-intensive tasks where high RAM density is unnecessary, making it well fitted for software compilation, CI/CD pipelines, static web traffic, and microservices.
